newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-London oil exchange hit over rules failure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-London oil exchange hit over rules failure.

text.p: London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) on Thursday came in for sharp criticism for failing to enforce its own rules.
An independent review, commissioned by the exchange, also said the IPE had proved unwilling to stand up to the interests of some its biggest customers, large oil trading companies.

"The IPE needs to be a stronger enforcer of rules, be more consistent in applying its rules and be less susceptible to trader pressure," the report's author, independent energy consultant Sally Clubley, said in an interview.

The IPE, the world's second largest oil futures exchange after NYMEX in the United States, asked Clubley to examine the way its gas oil (heating oil) futures contract is traded after a row between two trading houses last November caused severe disruption to Europe's main winter energy market.
The review recommended that the IPE took action to reduce potential market manipulation by introducing limits on the number of contracts that traders could hold.
It said problems surrounding IPE contracts had reached the stage where they had been made less effective as hedging instruments.
Clubley, a former member of the exchange's board, aimed the brunt of her criticism at the IPE's inability to patrol its members' activities.
"A lot of the rules are already in place, but they are not enforced strongly enough -- the IPE needs to be seen to be fair and consistent," she said.
Taking soundings from a wide cross-section of market participants Clubley said the IPE often failed to resist pressure from bigger trading groups.
"I think they have perhaps listened too closely to the large players which is one of the reasons smaller players have reduced hedging activities."
Another frequent complaint from users of the IPE was of inexperienced staff who did not have the expertise to understand some of the ramifications of trading positions.
The market is concerned that "the IPE does not have staff with the experience of the physical market," the review report said.
Aside from suggesting a tougher enforcement policy the report recommended a number of other changes.
The IPE said it was considering the recommendations and was taking comments from the market before formulating specific proposals for changes or clarifications to its procedures in May.
"We are ready to make changes," IPE chief executive Lynton Jones told Reuters.
"If that is the perception of the market then clearly we have to do something about it," Jones said in response to the criticism of staff expertise.
Clubley said the IPE was already acting to tighten up some regulations.
"They are beefing up compliance and are appointing a lawyer to look at rewriting some of the regulations," she said.
The IPE review comes in the wake of a string of reforms at London's other big commodity exchange, the London Metal Exchange.
British regulator the Securities and Investments Board told the LME last year to become more transparent and vigilant in the wake of a multi-billion dollar Sumitomo copper scandal.
